newsitem.title: USA: Capital flows show need for sound policy - W.Bank.
newsitem.headline: Capital flows show need for sound policy - W.Bank.

text.p: Increasing investment flows to developing nations expose them to new volatility and highlight their need for sound banking and capital market regulation, World Bank economic advisor Amar Battacharya said.

Increasing integration with the industrialized world leaves developing states vulnerable to capital flight and magnifies the costs of their own policy mistakes, Bhattacharya said Thursday in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.

"In many developing countries the banking systems are not up to the task of intermediating large inflows of private capital," said Bhattarchya, the principal author of a World Bank study on private capital mobility to be released at 1500 EST/1900 GMT.

"What integration does is that when investors lose confidence, the rug is pulled out very quickly under you so that you find yourself facing a situation as Mexico saw in 1994 or as some others are seeing right now," he added.
Bhattacharya said the Bank was also concerned that governments should not give excessive insurance to private investors.
The danger of government guarantees and subsidies masked as incentives to privately-funded projects is being examined at a World Bank conference in Colombia this week.

"It is not a serious problem now, but we think there could be significant chances of debt defaults say 15 years down the road... and we want to point out ways to stop this happening," World Bank economist Mateen Thobani told Reuters Wednesday.
But with proper use of capital reserves and the right balance between free markets and government guarantees and subsidies, developing nations can mimimize default risks, Bhattacharya said.
"(Default) is a risk that everybody should be worrying about, and the more people worry about it, the less the risk," he added.

Asked about current account deficit problems plaguing the Czech Republic and Thailand, Bhattacharya said a tactical approach involving adequate fiscal reserves and modernized banking systems can help nations ride out crises.

"Market discipline is much more stringent on the way out, meaning when investor confidence is lost, than in the buildup to a potential problem, which means that for governments, it's much more important to take a prudent approach," he added.
